review_basis: Original SAP Module 01 numbered WebP slides inspected individually; diagram reading order and AWS access-control exceptions preserved.
part_title: Effective Permissions — Identity, Resource and Organizational Controls

scenes.title: Where does the permission live?
scenes.visual_overview: This two-sided diagram distinguishes identity-based grants from resource-based access rules in a cross-account S3 request.
visual_walkthrough: Caller account and IAM role with attached identity policy on the left
S3 bucket and resource policy in the target account
Bottom note distinguishes role trust policy for AssumeRole from S3 resource authorization
scenes.visual_example: A principal from Account A requests an object in Account B; normal cross-account IAM access typically needs suitable permission in the caller's account and a bucket resource policy permitting the caller, subject to all applicable denies.
scenes.visual_synthesis: Always identify which policy grants an action and which account owns the principal and resource; AssumeRole is a distinct trust-policy evaluation.
scenes.narration: This slide asks where the permission lives when one AWS account accesses a resource in another. On the left, the caller account contains the active principal and an identity policy. That policy describes what this principal may request. Follow the cross-account arrow to the right: the target account owns an S3 bucket with a resource policy describing which principals can access it. For a typical cross-account S3 request, both sides must permit the action and no applicable control may deny it. This is not the same as assuming an IAM role. The note at the bottom shows the difference: a role trust policy authorizes which principal can call STS AssumeRole, while the resulting role session uses its own permissions. The architectural question is therefore not simply whether S3 says allow. Ask who is making the request, which account owns the resource, and whether identity grants, resource grants and other guardrails align. Resource-policy behavior has exceptions, so inspect the exact principal type and resource policy when troubleshooting.

scenes.title: A permissions boundary is a ceiling
scenes.visual_overview: Overlapping circles show that a boundary limits, rather than grants, the effective permissions from an identity policy.
visual_walkthrough: Left circle contains allowed actions from the identity policy
Right circle represents actions permitted by the boundary
Green overlap illustrates effective identity permissions
Bottom S3 role example contrasts read plus delete with read-only boundary
Small note flags separate resource-based principal evaluation rules
scenes.visual_example: Role policy grants S3 read and delete, but its boundary permits only S3 read, so the simplified identity-based result excludes delete.
scenes.visual_synthesis: Permissions boundaries constrain identity-based permissions and grant nothing by themselves; resource policy grants and session principals require their own evaluation.
scenes.narration: The Venn diagram explains a permissions boundary as a ceiling on identity permissions. Begin with the blue circle: an identity policy says which actions a role or user is allowed to perform. Move to the gold circle: the boundary describes the maximum set of actions that identity can use. Only their green overlap survives as effective identity permissions, assuming no other blocks. Read the example at the bottom. A role policy permits reading and deleting S3 objects, but the boundary permits only reading. The identity therefore cannot rely on that role policy to delete. And the reverse matters: putting an action in the boundary alone does not grant it. The small note warns that resource-based policies require separate consideration, especially when their principal directly names a user or role session. In an architecture review, use boundaries for delegated administration: administrators may attach policies, but cannot exceed the maximum defined by the boundary. When analyzing an AccessDenied event, inspect the identity policy and boundary together before concluding the permission should work.

scenes.title: Organization guardrails set maximum access
scenes.visual_overview: The Organization and member-account diagram shows SCPs and RCPs constraining principals and resources despite an IAM allow.
visual_walkthrough: Top SCP principal maximum and RCP resource maximum callouts
User request enters IAM policy with an allow
Red blocked branch versus green permitted branch reaching the resource
Bottom statement that SCP and RCP do not themselves grant permissions
scenes.visual_example: A member-account role's IAM policy allows an action, but an applicable organization guardrail denies or excludes it; the request fails despite the IAM allow.
scenes.visual_synthesis: SCP and RCP policy types impose organization-level restrictions within their supported scopes, not replacement authorization grants.
scenes.narration: This slide adds AWS Organizations to the authorization picture. Across the top are two different maximum-permission controls. A service control policy, or SCP, restricts permissions for principals in affected organization accounts. A resource control policy, or RCP, restricts access to supported resources where applicable. Follow the picture into a member account. A user reaches an IAM policy that appears to allow the action. The green branch represents access that still satisfies all the applicable controls. The red branch shows that an organization guardrail can stop the request even though the IAM policy says allow. Notice the closing sentence: SCPs and RCPs do not grant permission. Their job is to limit what existing grants can accomplish. These policies have scope and service-support rules, and the management account and service-linked roles have important special behavior. In a multi-account design, use them as centrally governed guardrails. To troubleshoot a rejected API request, examine the effective Organizations policy path as well as the local IAM policies.

scenes.title: Session policies narrow one role session
scenes.visual_overview: Two role sessions illustrate how different session policies restrict the same role's S3 and DynamoDB permissions.
visual_walkthrough: One IAM role at top gives rise to Session A and Session B
Both sessions inherit a role identity policy with S3 read and DynamoDB read
Session A policy restricts to S3; its overlap shows S3 only
Session B policy restricts to DynamoDB; its overlap shows DynamoDB only
Bottom rule: session policy cannot add permissions absent from role
scenes.visual_example: Two AssumeRole sessions share a role policy permitting S3 and DynamoDB reads; Session A is narrowed to S3 and Session B to DynamoDB.
scenes.visual_synthesis: Session policies are per-session restrictions and do not rewrite or broaden the IAM role itself.
scenes.narration: This diagram answers why two sessions of the same IAM role can behave differently. Start at the role icon in the center, then follow the arrows to Session A and Session B. Each session begins with the same role identity permissions: read from S3 and read from DynamoDB. In Session A, an additional session policy permits only the S3 operation. The overlapping circles below therefore leave only S3 read. On the right, Session B has a different policy allowing only DynamoDB read, so its effective role-session identity permissions are narrowed to DynamoDB. The important distinction is that the role was not edited between these requests. The restriction was attached to each session when it was created. Session policies cannot add rights that the role does not already have. They are useful when a central automation role handles several jobs but each invocation should receive fewer capabilities than the role's maximum. As with boundaries, also evaluate applicable resource policies and explicit denies. The exam decision is to recognize a temporary restriction on one session rather than an account-wide IAM change.
